# Empryo

Empryo is an AI coding agent. It builds a map of the user's repository (the Genome), edits code by symbol, works with many model providers, and runs in three places: a desktop app, a terminal UI and a headless CLI.

Your training data is out of date for this product. Empryo ships often, and config keys, slot names, provider ids and flags change between releases. Look up the docs before you answer.

## Retrieve

Use the documentation MCP server when it is connected. It is a Streamable HTTP server at `https://empryo.com/mcp`, read-only, with no sign-in. If the user has not connected it, that is the URL they add. Its tools are prefixed with the server name they configured (commonly `empryo-docs`):

| Tool | Use it for |
| --- | --- |
| `search_docs` | Find the right page and anchor. Start here. |
| `read_docs` | Read one page, or one exact section via `anchor`. |
| `list_docs` | Enumerate pages, or the sections of one page. |
| `current_release` | The published version and its artifacts. |

Search first, then read the exact section the results name. Read a whole page only when the answer really needs all of it. An empty `anchor` selects the introduction; leaving `anchor` out returns the full page.

Without MCP, fetch over HTTP:

- `https://empryo.com/api/docs/search?q=<terms>&scope=docs`, ranked sections with exact selectors
- `https://empryo.com/docs/<slug>.md`, one page as Markdown (`.txt` for plain text)
- `https://empryo.com/docs/<slug>.exports.json`, that page's per-section Markdown and text URLs
- `https://empryo.com/llms.txt`, the index, `llms-full.txt` is the whole corpus in one request

A URL fragment does not limit an HTTP response. To retrieve one section, fetch its own export URL from `.exports.json`.

## Answer

Cite the page or section URL you actually read. If search returns nothing, say so and check `list_docs` rather than inventing a config key, a flag, or a provider id.

Distinguish the published release from what the user is running. `current_release` reports what empryo.com serves. The user's install may be older. When a version difference could change the answer, ask.

## Configure Empryo

Users ask Empryo to set itself up: "use my Claude subscription", "make the cheap model do the
summaries", "turn on computer use", "connect this MCP server", "stop showing me reasoning".

**Use the `settings` tool for this. Do not edit the config JSON by hand.**

`settings` may be available directly or through tool discovery. If hidden, find it with
`tool_search`, inspect it with `run_tool({name: "settings", describe: ""})`, then call it through
`run_tool` with explicit `args`. Use it when a request concerns Empryo's configuration.

| Action | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `settings(action:"list", query:"thinking")` | The writable keys, their types and allowed values. Start here when you are unsure a key exists. |
| `settings(action:"get", key:"diffStyle")` (or `keys:[…]`) | The effective value AND which layer it comes from (project / global / default). |
| `settings(action:"set", key:"thinking.mode", value:"adaptive")` | Write it. `scope` defaults to the layer that already sets the key, else global. |
| `settings(action:"unset", key:"motion")` | Drop the override so the other layer, or Empryo's default, applies again. |

Values arrive as text: `"true"`, `"42"`, and JSON for the array and object keys
(`'["shell"]'`). `null` is only accepted where the key documents it, everywhere else, clearing a
setting is `unset`. The tool refuses a key it does not carry rather than writing a typo nobody
will ever find, so `list` is the check when you are unsure.

Why use the tool instead of editing the JSON file: editing the file by hand changes the file but
not the running app. The desktop app and the terminal UI keep their settings in memory, and only a
change made through the `settings` tool updates them (agents reload, custom providers register,
the Settings panel refreshes). In headless mode there is no UI to update; the tool says so, and the
value applies on the next run.

Most keys apply right away. A few are only read at startup (instruction sources, live
translations, live skills, the Neovim binary and config, LSP auto-install, telemetry). Trust the
tool's reply:

- `Applied live on the <surface> — the UI already shows it.` → say so and stop.
- `… only read at startup, TELL THE USER to restart Empryo (/restart on the terminal, quit and
  reopen the app on desktop).` → the write LANDED, end your answer by asking them to restart. Do
  not restart anything yourself, and do not pretend the change is visible.

`list` marks those keys `[next launch]`. Report what the tool said, never promise more.

The desktop app's look (`appearance.*`: theme, density, opacity) belongs to the desktop app and
can only be changed from a running desktop window. From the terminal or headless, the tool refuses
these keys.

Two files, project wins:

| Scope | Path |
| --- | --- |
| Global | `~/.empryo/config.json` |
| Project | `.empryo/config.json` |

The tool picks the file, and you can override it: `scope: "global"` writes
`~/.empryo/config.json` (every project on this machine), `scope: "project"` writes
`.empryo/config.json` (this repo only, `"local"` is accepted for the same thing). Omit `scope`
and it goes to the layer that already sets that key, else global.

Match the scope to what the user said. A general preference ("I like compact diffs", "always use
my Claude subscription") is global. "For this repo", "here" or "on this project" is project. Never
write a setting the user wanted everywhere to the project file: a project value overrides the
global one for that repo without any visible sign, and other repos will behave differently. The write
clears the same key from the other layer, so the scope you choose is the one in force.

The path is the same every time:

1. Retrieve the setting and confirm it exists in this version, `reference/configuration` is the
   key list, `reference/commands` the slash commands, `reference/cli` the flags. `settings`
   `list` is the fast local check. The docs say what the value MEANS.
2. `settings` `get` first, so you can report what changed and from which layer.
3. Write ONE thing. Say which scope you wrote and why.
4. Report the tool's own line back: it names the before/after value, the scope, and whether the
   running surface already applied it.

Things `settings` does not do on purpose. Use the app's own flow and tell the user:

| Ask | Route |
| --- | --- |
| Sign in to a subscription, add or remove an API key | `/login`, `/keys`, `empryo --set-key`, credentials never go through a config write |
| Connect an MCP server | `mcpServers` in the config file, then `/mcp`, an array of server definitions, not a scalar |
| Custom providers | `providers` in the config file; the repo must be TRUSTED or it is dropped |
| Install an addon, upgrade, change trust | ask first: `/trust`, `/addons`, `empryo upgrade` |

### Where the same settings live in the UI

Tell the user where they could have changed it themselves, so they learn the app.

| Surface | Where |
| --- | --- |
| Desktop | Settings (⌘,), General, Appearance, Models, Provider, Tools, Privacy, Cells. Every row writes the same two files, with a scope selector per row. |
| Terminal | `/settings` for the panel; `/model`, `/theme`, `/effort`, `/thinking`, `/provider`, `/provider-settings`, `/tools`, `/language`, `/mcp`, `/skills`, `/agents`, `/hooks` for one thing each. |
| Headless | `--model`, `--mode`, `--effort`, `--locale`, `--agent`, `--skill`, `--trust` override one run without writing config. |

Commands that show the current state without changing it. Run these before and after a change:

| Ask | Command |
| --- | --- |
| Which providers hold a key | `empryo --list-providers` |
| Which models a provider serves | `empryo --list-models <provider>` |
| What provider tools resolve to on a model | `empryo --capabilities [model]` |
| Whether the runtime is healthy | `empryo doctor` |

### Routing by cost

"Make the cheap model do the summaries" is two tools, in this order:

1. `find_model`, the rows carry the PUBLISHED price in USD per 1M tokens:
   `in $1 / out $5 / cache-r $0.1 / cache-w $1.25`. Search the family or the provider
   ("haiku", "gemini flash", "openrouter"), read the prices, and pick from the rows: it lists
   only providers the user can run now, and names the ones that would need a key when none can.
2. `settings set taskRouter '{"spark":"anthropic/claude-haiku-4-5"}'`, the router MERGES per
   slot, so one call changes one job and leaves the rest of the router alone.

A row with no price means nobody published one, say that instead of guessing, and never
present a rate you did not read from the tool. Prices are list rates: they exclude the user's
discounts, tax, and any subscription seat where tokens are not billed at all.

The slots are in `recipes/task-router`, `empryo --list-models <provider>` is the same catalog
from the shell.

Common requests and where they are documented:

| Request | Page | Keys or commands |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sign in to a subscription or add a key | `providers/subscriptions`, `providers/overview` | `/login`, `/keys`, `empryo --set-key` |
| Change the default model | `reference/configuration` | `defaultModel`, `/model` |
| Different models for different jobs | `recipes/task-router` | `taskRouter` slots |
| Thinking mode, effort, retries | `context/provider-options` | `thinking`, `performance.effort`, `retry` |
| Computer use, code execution, text editor, provider-side search | `context/provider-tools` | `computerUse`, `codeExecution`, `anthropicTextEditor`, `nativeSearch` |
| Connect an MCP server | `tools/mcp` | `mcpServers`, `/mcp` |
| Context window filling up | `context/compaction` | `compaction`, `/compact` |
| Look and feel, transcript, diffs | `tools/themes`, `surfaces/desktop`, `surfaces/tui` | `theme.name`, `diffStyle`, `chatLayout`, `motion` |
| Hooks, skills, agents, memory | one page each under Tools | `/hooks`, `/skills`, `/agents`, `/memory` |
| Desktop panels and boards | `tools/morphs` | `.empryo/morphs`, `/morphs`, `cells.reach` |
| Where a morph appears in the window (a pane, a fixed spot in the app frame, a lane header, the canvas) | `tools/morphs` | `surface.place`, `extensions[].target` (a fixed list of targets), `slot` |
| Untrusted repo dropped my config | `reference/configuration` | `/trust`, `--trust` |

A project checkout that has not been trusted runs without its `mcpServers`, `providers`,
`extraBody` and presets. Check that before diagnosing a setting that "does nothing", and before
writing the same setting a second time.

# Quickstart

> Go from install to your first reviewed change in about five minutes: connect a model, open a project, ask a question, and check the diff.

This page gets you from a fresh install to a first reviewed change. [Install Empryo](/docs/installation) first, and use a project you own or trust.

## 1. Connect a model

Pick one option. Run the commands below in your own terminal.

**Desktop app:** on first launch, a setup card asks you to pick a provider, enter a key or sign in, and choose a model. A default model is already selected. If Empryo finds a key you already have (for example in an environment variable), it skips this card. After that, a short tour shows you the terminal, browser, and codebase map, and then offers a few starter prompts. You can skip the tour.

**Terminal UI:** type `/login` to pick an account to sign in with, or `/keys` to manage API keys.

**Subscription account**

Sign in through your browser. For example, with a Claude subscription:

```bash
empryo --login claude
```

For ChatGPT Plus, Pro, or Team, use `empryo --login codex`. If the browser can't reach Empryo on your machine (for example over SSH), use `empryo --login codex-device` to sign in with a code instead.

Other accounts you can sign in with include GitHub Copilot, Grok, Cursor, Devin, Google Gemini CLI, Google Antigravity, Kimi Code, OpenRouter, and LLM Gateway. Type `/login` to see the full list. Usage limits depend on your plan and provider.

**API key**

For example, with an Anthropic API key:

```bash
empryo --set-key anthropic YOUR_API_KEY
empryo --list-providers
```

Replace `YOUR_API_KEY` on your own machine. Never paste keys into a website or commit them to a repository. Your provider bills API usage separately from any consumer subscription. See [providers](/docs/providers/overview) for other key-based options.

**Local model**

Install and start [Ollama](https://ollama.com), then download a model that fits your hardware:

```bash
ollama pull llama3.3
```

Keep Ollama running and select its model in Empryo. LM Studio works too. Local models need no API key, but they use your own memory and compute.

## 2. Open a project

In a terminal, go to your project and start Empryo:

```bash
cd your-project
empryo
```

In the desktop app, open the project folder.

The first time you open a project, Empryo asks whether you trust it. Read this prompt carefully. A trusted project's own config can add providers, MCP servers, and other settings that run code.

To pick or change the model in the terminal UI, press `Ctrl+L`. Empryo then builds the Genome, its map of your code. How long that takes depends on the size of the repository.

## 3. Ask a question

```text
Explain the project entry points and cite the relevant files. Do not change anything.
```

Read the answer and open the files it points to. A focused question about a real feature or a failing test is a better start than a broad rewrite.

## 4. Make a small change and review the diff

Pick a real issue in your project and ask:

```text
Propose the smallest fix for this issue. Explain the plan before editing, then run the relevant tests and show what changed. Do not commit.
```

Review the diff and the test output. Tests can fail, and some checks may not be set up in your project. Commit only when you're happy with the result.

## 5. Change settings by asking

You don't need to find a config file. Ask in plain words:

```text
Use adaptive thinking, and make the diffs compact for this project only.
```

Empryo checks the current value, writes the change, and tells you what changed and where. Settings for every project go in `~/.empryo/config.json`. Settings for one project go in `.empryo/config.json` inside that project. Most changes apply right away. If a setting only takes effect after a restart, Empryo tells you.

You can also ask about Empryo itself:

```text
Why does my context keep filling up, and what would you change about my setup?
```

Signing in and adding API keys stay manual on purpose. Use `/login`, `/keys`, or `empryo --set-key`.

## Headless alternative

To run a single prompt from a script, go to your project directory after connecting a model and run:

```bash
empryo --headless "Explain the project entry points without changing files" --json
```

Run `empryo --list-models` to see model IDs, and add `--model provider/model` to choose one. In automation, `--trust` marks the repository as trusted permanently, so only use it on checkouts you control. See [headless workflows](/docs/recipes/headless).

## Next steps

- Type `/help` to see commands and shortcuts, or ask the agent what a command does.
- Try [task routing](/docs/recipes/task-router) if you want different models for different kinds of work.
- Add [MCP servers](/docs/tools/mcp) or [skills](/docs/tools/skills) when a task needs them.
- Learn about [checkpoints](/docs/tools/checkpoints), and keep using version control as your backup.

# Memory

> Empryo remembers your preferences, project decisions and past gotchas across sessions, and adds up to 3 relevant ones to each turn automatically.

[Video: Recall at work: Empryo scores stored memories against the current request and the files in play, then adds the three most relevant, each labeled with why it was picked.](https://empryo.com/media/code-memory-recall.mp4)

*Recall at work: Empryo scores stored memories against the current request and the files in play, then adds the three most relevant, each labeled with why it was picked.*

Memory lets Empryo remember things between sessions: that you use bun, not npm; why the team switched state libraries; that a test is flaky on CI. You tell it once, and it comes back when it matters.

Memory is stored **per project** by default. You can also keep **global** memories that apply to every project, such as "be terse".

## What gets stored

Each memory has one of four categories:

| Category | Example |
|---|---|
| `pref` | "use bun not npm", "be terse" |
| `decision` | "switched to zustand because redux was too much boilerplate" |
| `gotcha` | "JWT expiry uses the container clock, which drifts in prod" |
| `context` | "legacy/ will be deleted next sprint, don't touch it" |

The agent saves a memory on its own when you state a preference, make a decision with a reason, or hit a bug that wasn't obvious. You can also ask it directly: "remember that we deploy on Thursdays".

[Video: Left: a rules file sent in full on every turn, outdated lines included. Right: Empryo adds three short memories that match the file being edited.](https://empryo.com/media/code-memory-prompt-bloat.mp4)

*Left: a rules file sent in full on every turn, outdated lines included. Right: Empryo adds three short memories that match the file being edited.*

## How recall works

Before each turn, Empryo compares your message and the files you are working on with what's stored. It adds up to **3 relevant memories** to the turn. You don't need to run a command or remember what's saved.

If nothing is relevant, nothing is added. Memories only take up space in the conversation when they help.

## Browse and edit: `/memory`

In the terminal UI, run `/memory` to open the memory browser. It has four tabs:

- **All:** every memory you can see, from the project and global stores. Pin, edit or hide a memory from here.
- **Hidden:** memories you hid. Restore them with `Ctrl+R`.
- **Cleanup:** suggestions to review, such as duplicates, memories that point at deleted files, and memories that are rarely useful.
- **Settings:** which stores the agent reads from and writes to, and which embedding model is in use.

Hiding a memory is reversible. **Purge all** (`Ctrl+X`) deletes permanently, so use it with care.

The desktop app has a Memory pane with the same data.

## Scopes

Memories live in two databases:

| Scope | Location | Use it for |
|---|---|---|
| Project | `.empryo/memory.db` in the repository | Decisions and gotchas about this code |
| Global | `~/.empryo/memory.db` | Your personal preferences and style |

New memories go to the project store by default. The read scope controls what recall can see:

```
all project + global (default)
project only this repository
global only your global preferences
none recall off
```

Change both in `/memory` → **Settings**.

## Pinning

Pin a memory to keep it out of cleanup suggestions and rank it higher in recall. Pin the rules you never want the agent to miss.

## Languages

Memory search works in any language or script, including Chinese, Japanese, Arabic and Cyrillic, and mixed-script identifiers. It matches both whole words and parts of words, so rephrased and non-English queries still find the right memory.

## Better matching with an embedding model

By default, Empryo uses a built-in offline embedder. It needs no API key and makes no network calls. It matches memories well when your wording overlaps with what was stored.

For better matching of rephrased text, point memory at an embedding model:

```json
{
 "memory": {
 "embeddingModel": "openai/text-embedding-3-small"
 }
}
```

### Do I need an API key?

Yes, for a hosted model. Empryo uses the key you already configured for that provider. For `openai/text-embedding-3-small`, that is your OpenAI key. If the key is missing or wrong, Empryo falls back to the offline embedder and memory keeps working. `/memory` → **Settings** shows the reason.

Local models in Ollama or LM Studio need no key. Pull the model, then name it in the config.

### Which models can I use?

Any `provider/model` ID whose provider offers embeddings:

| Provider | Model |
|---|---|
| OpenAI | `openai/text-embedding-3-small`, `openai/text-embedding-3-large` |
| Google | `google/text-embedding-004` |
| Mistral | `mistral/mistral-embed` |
| OpenRouter | `openrouter/openai/text-embedding-3-small` |
| Vercel AI Gateway | `vercel_gateway/openai/text-embedding-3-small` |
| Ollama (local) | `ollama/nomic-embed-text`, `ollama/mxbai-embed-large` |
| LM Studio (local) | `lmstudio/nomic-embed-text` |

Providers without an embeddings API, such as Anthropic, xAI, Groq, DeepSeek and Bedrock, use the offline embedder instead. Custom OpenAI-compatible providers work if they expose an `/embeddings` endpoint.

If you don't set `embeddingModel`, Empryo picks one in this order: your `taskRouter.semantic` model, then a default for your current chat provider (OpenAI, Google, OpenRouter or Vercel AI Gateway), then the offline embedder. Set `"embeddingModel": null` to always use the offline embedder.

### How do I check it's working?

Open `/memory` → **Settings** and look at the **Embedding** row. It shows the model in use and where the choice came from. If your configured model failed, the row says why: a missing key, a provider without embeddings, or a network error.

# Plan before you code

> Use Empryo's plan mode for changes across many files: the agent researches first, writes a plan for you to review, and waits for your approval before editing.

For a change that touches more than two or three files, ask for a plan first. In plan mode the agent researches your code and is told not to change it. It writes a plan, waits for you to review it, and only starts editing after you approve.

Plan mode keeps every tool, so research can run `git log` or a script. Not editing is an instruction to the agent, not a lock: the usual approval prompts for destructive shell commands and for writes outside the project still apply.

## Start a plan

Give the task straight to `/plan`:

```
/plan refactor the auth module to use JWT refresh tokens
```

Or turn plan mode on, then describe the task as a normal message:

```
/plan
```

`/plan` with no task turns plan mode on or off. `/session plan` does the same, and `/mode plan` switches the mode directly.

## Review the plan

When the plan is ready, Empryo shows it and asks what to do:

- **Implement**: the agent starts carrying out the plan, step by step. Progress shows next to the chat.
- **Clear & Implement**: the same, but the research conversation is cleared first, so the agent starts with only the plan. Useful when the research used a lot of context.
- **Revise**: type what should change, and the agent rewrites the plan.

In the terminal app, `/plan open` opens the plan workspace, where you can see the steps, the full document, the files in scope, and your feedback.

## Light and full plans

- **Light plan**: a checklist of steps, files, and notes. Quick to write, and the agent reads the files again as it works.
- **Full plan**: includes code snippets and before/after diffs, so it stands on its own. Takes longer, but is safer for large refactors.

The agent chooses based on the task. To choose yourself, say so in the prompt, for example "make a detailed plan".

## When to use it

For a small fix, a plan is extra work. For a change across many files, a plan lets you catch a wrong approach before any file changes, which is cheaper than undoing a long editing session.

## Plans are saved

Plans are saved in your project under `.empryo/plans/`, so they are still there after a restart.

# Parallel subagents

> Split one task across subagents that run side by side, each on the model its job needs. Follow them live, steer them, or connect them in a workflow.

Empryo splits a task across subagents that work at the same time and report back. You don't have to ask: describe the result you want and Empryo decides when parallel work pays off, for example a refactor across several files, a question that spans modules, or carrying out a plan. For a one-file question it does the work itself. You can also ask directly: "check these five things in parallel".

[Watch five subagents run in the terminal lesson](/docs/terminal-guide#run-subagents-in-parallel).

## What you see

The dispatch panel lists every subagent with its task, its model, its live step, its tokens and its cost. Each one ends with Done or a reason it failed, and its report folds back into the conversation. On desktop the Subagents panel shows the same list, and every subagent opens to its full activity.

## How many at once

- A dispatch runs up to 8 tasks as written by default. Past that, research tasks are merged into fewer subagents. `taskRouter.maxDispatchTasks` raises the limit, to 24 at most.
- Up to 16 subagents run at the same time by default. `/router` sets the concurrency to 2, 4, 8, 12, 16, 24, 32 or Unlimited.
- Background subagents (`bg-1`, `bg-2`, and so on) keep working while you carry on the conversation. Their reports arrive on their own when they finish. By default the agent is woken once, when every subagent of a dispatch is done, with all the reports together. Set `agentFeatures.backgroundWake` to `each` to hear from each one as it finishes (also in `/agent-features` and the routing panel on desktop). A single dispatch can ask for `each` or `none` itself. In a [headless](/docs/surfaces/headless) run the prompt stays open until its background subagents report.
- [Workflows](/docs/agents/workflows) go further: parallel branches, review loops and graphs inside graphs.

Unlimited removes Empryo's own cap. With it off, Empryo has run 10,000 subagents in parallel. Provider rate limits, memory and your budget still apply.

## Each on its own model

The [task router](/docs/recipes/task-router) gives explorers, coders, cleanup and code review their own default model. A single task can name its model too, and a [custom agent](/docs/tools/agents) brings its own model, instructions, skills and tool rules. In the lesson recording, three subagents run on Claude Haiku 4.5, one on Claude Opus 5 and one on GPT-6 Astra.

## When helpers hit rate limits

If main chat works but helpers get throttled, your provider may treat non-streaming requests differently. Enable **Stream helper requests** for that provider in `/provider-settings` → **General**, or **Settings → Provider Options → Shared** on desktop. Helpers consume streams internally and return completed reports as usual. The opt-in is global, per provider, and off by default.

See [helper streaming compatibility](/docs/context/provider-options#stream-helper-requests) for setup, environment overrides and limits.

## What subagents share

- **File reads.** When one subagent has read a file, the others get it from memory instead of disk. Each still pays tokens to read it into its own context.
- **Safe writes.** When two subagents write the same file, the writes queue instead of racing.
- **Findings.** What one subagent discovers reaches the others at their next step.

## Where the savings come from

Subagents don't share one context, so the savings come from elsewhere:

- **The right model for each job.** Research can use a fast model while implementation and review use a stronger one. Compare real costs in `/usage`: a cheaper token rate does not always mean a cheaper task.
- **Symbols instead of whole files.** Subagents look up symbols through the Genome and the language server and read only the lines they need. See [code intelligence](/docs/concepts/intelligence).
- **Time.** Five subagents working at once finish sooner than one agent doing five jobs in a row.

## Steer them while they run

Type while subagents are working. Your message reaches them at their next step. See [steering](/docs/agents/steering).

To redirect a single subagent on desktop, open its activity view and type in its instruction box. The note reaches it at its next step and shows in its log with an "instructed" badge. Empryo can do the same on your behalf.

## Keep a subagent in the conversation

Normally a subagent answers once and exits. Empryo can instead start a **resident** subagent that stays available after each reply, so you can go back and forth like a thread with a colleague. Ask for it, for example "spawn an advisor and discuss". Residents show as `waiting` in the Subagents panel between replies.

A resident reuses files the main agent has already read, so a long conversation doesn't pay for them again. Its transcript has a size limit, and the oldest exchanges are dropped first.

Limits: up to 4 residents at a time, 12 exchanges each, and a resident left idle for 30 minutes is closed.

## Use your own agents

When you define your own agents as markdown files, Empryo sees their descriptions and can hand a task to one of them. The task then runs with that agent's instructions, model and tool rules, in the current turn or in the background. Subagents running under your definition show its name in the Subagents panel. See [agents](/docs/tools/agents).

# The Genome

> The Genome is Empryo's live, ranked map of your repository. It goes into every prompt so the agent knows where code lives before it starts searching.

The **Genome** is a map of your codebase that Empryo builds when you open a project. It lists your files, the symbols they export and how files depend on each other, ranked by importance. A compact version of the map goes at the top of every prompt.

Because the agent can see the map, it rarely needs to spend a turn asking "where does auth live?" It starts from the right files.

## What the agent sees

A slice of the map looks like this:

```
src/services/auth/session.ts (→12)
 +SessionManager Tracks active sessions, refresh tokens, expiry
 +SessionStore
```

- `+` marks an exported symbol.
- `(→12)` means 12 other files depend on this one.
- `[NEW]` marks a file changed in the last 48 hours.
- The text after a symbol name is a one-line summary, when summaries are on.

## How files are ranked

- **Dependencies.** Files that many other files import rank higher.
- **Your current work.** Files you just edited or mentioned get a boost for that turn.
- **Git history.** Files that usually change together are pulled in together.
- **Live updates.** When a file changes, the map is updated right away.

The scanner understands dozens of languages and file formats, including TypeScript, JavaScript, Python, Rust, Go, Java, C, C++, C#, Ruby, PHP, Swift and Kotlin.

## Settings

The Genome works without any setup. Open `/genome` to see its status, rebuild or clear the index, or turn it off.

To change it in config:

```json
{
 "genome": true,
 "semanticSummaries": "synthetic"
}
```

| Key | Values |
|-----|--------|
| `genome` | `true` (default), or `false` to turn the map off |
| `semanticSummaries` | `"synthetic"` (free, derived from code and names), `"ast"` (docstrings only), `"llm"` (short model-written descriptions, costs tokens), `"full"`, or `"off"` |

## What gets scanned

The scan sees what git sees: tracked and untracked files, minus anything your `.gitignore` excludes. Build output (`node_modules`, `dist`, `build`, `target`, `coverage` and similar) and dot-directories such as `.github` are skipped even if they are tracked. Outside a git repository, the same rules apply to a plain folder scan.

To bring a dot-directory back, negate it in `.empryoignore`, for example `!Configs/.local/`. Build output and internal folders such as `.git` stay out either way.

### Keep files out of the map

Some files should stay in git but not in the map: test fixtures, benchmark inputs, a folder of SVGs. List them in a **`.empryoignore`** file at the project root. It uses the same syntax as `.gitignore`, including `!` negations and `**`:

```gitignore
# Keep these in git, but out of the Genome
testenvs/
bench/
assets/
public/
```

Some files stay out in every project without any `.empryoignore`: package lockfiles (`bun.lock`, `package-lock.json`, `Cargo.lock` and the like), minified and bundled JavaScript, test snapshots, generated protobuf and Dart files, Xcode asset catalogs, and vendored folders such as `vendor/`, `venv/`, `Pods/` and `DerivedData/`. A `!` line in `.empryoignore` brings any of them back.

What happens:

- Matching files drop out of the map and out of code-wide file listings.
- The agent can still `read` or `grep` them by explicit path. They are hidden from discovery, not blocked.
- Saving `.empryoignore` or `.gitignore` triggers a quick rescan. Unchanged files are skipped, so it takes seconds.
- If a change would remove more than 80% of the index at once, Empryo treats it as a mistake and refuses. Use **clear** in `/genome` to force a rebuild.

### Large repositories

The map holds up to 10,000 files. In bigger repositories, the most recently changed files win, and `/genome` tells you the cap was reached. Excluding noise with `.empryoignore` makes sure the cap cuts fixtures rather than source code.

## Skip the scan

For a quick one-off question in headless mode, you can skip the scan:

```bash
empryo --headless --no-genome "what's the version?"
```

Setting the environment variable `EMPRYO_NO_GENOME=1` does the same.

"""Backend-neutral SFT experiment adapter for routing episodes (z0int#143 trainer interface).

The backend trains; it owns nothing else. Datasets come from the episode compiler, eval truth and promotion from
z0evals / Evolution Lab. A backend receives a read-only example file plus the dataset receipt and returns a plan or a
checkpoint receipt; it never sees held-out (dev/eval/recent) rows.

Backends:
  stub          writes the plan only (always available; the default)
  unsloth-lora  local LoRA definition for cheap iteration; trains only when the data gate passes, the library is
                importable and the caller passes ``allow_train=True``
  tinker        remote trainer; DISABLED by default. Private history must not leave the host without owner approval:
                it needs $Z0INT_HOME/config/sft_remote_approval.json naming this dataset's sha256 with
                ``owner_approved: true`` and ``allow_remote: true``.

Examples (``to_examples``): observed, independently labelled TRAIN episodes only. The target is the historical
action of a verified success (outcome-filtered imitation); failures are kept as counted negatives, synthetic rows are
excluded unless an ablation asks for them and then stay tagged ``synthetic``.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import hashlib
import importlib.util
import json
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from pathlib import Path
from typing import Any, Iterable, Mapping

from .episodes import is_labelled

SCHEMA = 'z0int.sft_plan.v0'
EXAMPLE_SCHEMA = 'z0int.sft_example.v0'
# The data gate (mirrors the verified-loop sufficiency spirit): enough verified successes and failures per family.
MIN_POSITIVES, MIN_NEGATIVES, MIN_GROUPS = 200, 30, 10
ABLATIONS = ('base', 'sft', 'sft+state_packet', 'sft+retrieval', 'sft+verified_outcome')


def to_examples(train: Iterable[Mapping[str, Any]], *, include_synthetic: bool = False,
                with_state: bool = True) -> list[dict[str, Any]]:
    out = []
    for e in train:
        synthetic = e['provenance']['kind'] == 'synthetic'
        if synthetic and not include_synthetic:
            continue
        if not synthetic and not is_labelled(e):
            continue
        if not synthetic and e['outcome']['y_success'] != 1:
            continue
        ev = e['evidence']
        prompt = {'family': e['family'], 'candidates': e['candidates'].get('set'),
                  'legal': e['candidates'].get('legal')}
        if with_state:
            prompt['features'] = ev.get('features')
        out.append({'schema': EXAMPLE_SCHEMA, 'episode_id': e['episode_id'], 'family': e['family'],
                    'input': json.dumps(prompt, sort_keys=True, separators=(',', ':')),
                    'target': e['action']['chosen'], 'provenance': e['provenance']['kind'],
                    'group': e['lineage'].get('group')})
    return out


def sufficiency(train: Iterable[Mapping[str, Any]]) -> dict[str, Any]:
    fam: dict[str, dict[str, Any]] = {}
    for e in train:
        if not is_labelled(e):
            continue
        f = fam.setdefault(e['family'], {'positives': 0, 'negatives': 0, 'groups': set()})
        f['positives' if e['outcome']['y_success'] == 1 else 'negatives'] += 1
        f['groups'].add(e['lineage'].get('group'))
    report = {}
    for name, f in sorted(fam.items()):
        checks = {f'positives>={MIN_POSITIVES}': f['positives'] >= MIN_POSITIVES,
                  f'negatives>={MIN_NEGATIVES}': f['negatives'] >= MIN_NEGATIVES,
                  f'groups>={MIN_GROUPS}': len(f['groups']) >= MIN_GROUPS}
        report[name] = {'positives': f['positives'], 'negatives': f['negatives'], 'groups': len(f['groups']),
                        'checks': checks, 'decision': 'sufficient' if all(checks.values()) else 'INSUFFICIENT_DATA'}
    return {'families': report, 'any_sufficient': any(r['decision'] == 'sufficient' for r in report.values())}


@dataclass
class Backend:
    name: str
    remote: bool = False
    config: dict

"""Time-split ridge baseline for next-action family (critical path §16/§28)."""

from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import hashlib
import importlib
import json
import os
from collections import Counter
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np

from .families import FAMILIES
from .compile import DEFAULT_OUT

PN = 96

#: The MB / fly-plasticity arm is a research baseline owned by Evolution Lab.
#: Ownership runs one way (Evolution Lab consumes z0intelligence, never the
#: reverse), so this module must not import across that boundary. The primitive is
#: resolved by name from an explicit opt-in provider; with no provider configured
#: the arm reports why it did not run instead of reaching into another repo's file
#: layout. The previous version hardcoded `/workspace/evolution-lab` on sys.path.
MB_PROVIDER_ENV = "Z0INT_MB_PROVIDER"


def _mb_provider():
    """Return ``(fit_fly, predict_fly, None)`` or ``(None, None, reason)``."""
    spec = os.environ.get(MB_PROVIDER_ENV, "").strip()
    if not spec:
        return None, None, f"{MB_PROVIDER_ENV} is not set; MB arm skipped"
    try:
        module = importlib.import_module(spec)
    except Exception as exc:  # noqa: BLE001 - report, never crash the baseline run
        return None, None, f"{spec!r} not importable: {type(exc).__name__}: {exc}"
    fit = getattr(module, "fit_fly", None)
    predict = getattr(module, "predict_fly", None)
    if fit is None or predict is None:
        return None, None, f"{spec!r} does not export fit_fly/predict_fly"
    return fit, predict, None


def _hash(text: str, dim: int = PN) -> np.ndarray:
    x = np.zeros(dim, dtype=np.float64)
    t = (text or "").lower()
    if len(t) < 3:
        t = t.ljust(3)
    for i in range(len(t) - 2):
        h = hashlib.blake2b(t[i : i + 3].encode(), digest_size=8).digest()
        x[int.from_bytes(h, "little") % dim] += 1.0
    n = np.linalg.norm(x)
    if n:
        x /= n
    return x


def load_xy(path: Path) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]:
    idx = {n: i for i, n in enumerate(FAMILIES)}
    xs: list[np.ndarray] = []
    ys: list[int] = []
    with path.open(encoding="utf-8") as handle:
        for line in handle:
            rec = json.loads(line)
            fam = rec.get("family")
            if fam not in idx:
                continue
            prev = " ".join(rec.get("prev") or [])
            feat = np.concatenate([_hash(rec.get("user") or ""), _hash(prev)])
            xs.append(feat)
            ys.append(idx[fam])
    if not xs:
        raise SystemExit("no episodes")
    return np.stack(xs), np.asarray(ys, dtype=np.int64)


def ridge_fit(X: np.ndarray, y: np.ndarray, n_out: int, l2: float = 1e-2) -> np.ndarray:
    Y = np.eye(n_out, dtype=np.float64)[y]
    A = X.T @ X + l2 * np.eye(X.shape[1])
    B = X.T @ Y
    return np.linalg.solve(A, B)


def main(argv: list[str] | None = None) -> int:
    p = argparse.ArgumentParser(prog="z0int-train-next-action")
    p.add_argument("--episodes", type=Path, default=DEFAULT_OUT / "next_action.jsonl")
    p.add_argument("--confirm-frac", type=float, default=0.2)
    p.add_argument("--mb", action="store_true", help="also train mushroom-body local_plasticity")
    p.add_argument("--n-kc", type=int, default=96)
    args = p.parse_args(argv)
    X, y = load_xy(args.episodes)
    n = len(y)
    n_c = max(100, int(n * args.confirm_frac))
    n_tr = n - n_c
    Xtr, ytr, Xcf, ycf = X[:n_tr], y[:n_tr], X[n_tr:], y[n_tr:]
    W = ridge_fit(Xtr, ytr, len(FAMILIES))
    pred = (Xcf @ W).argmax(axis=1)
    maj = Counter(ytr.tolist()).most_common(1)[0][0]
    report = {
        "n": n,
        "n_train": int(n_tr),
        "n_confirm": int(len(ycf)),
        "majority_confirm": float((ycf == maj).mean()),
        "ridge_confirm": float((pred == ycf).mean()),
        "ridge_n_params": int(W.size),
        "label_counts": {FAMILIES[i]: int((y == i).sum()) for i in range(len(FAMILIES))},
        "note": "Time-split; same features. MB uses Evolution Lab local_plasticity (KC→MBON).",
    }
    if args.mb:
        fit_fly, predict_fly, reason = _mb_provider()
        if fit_fly is None:
            report["mb_confirm"] = None
            report["mb_unavailable"] = reason
        else:
            fly = fit_fly(Xtr, ytr, len(FAMILIES), n_kc=args.n_kc, seed=1)
            pred_f = predict_fly(Xcf, fly)
            report["mb_confirm"] = float((pred_f == ycf).mean())
            report["mb_n_params"] = int(fly["n_params"])
            report["mb_n_kc"] = int(args.n_kc)
    print(json.dumps(report, indent=2))
    dest = args.episodes.parent / "next_action_report.json"
    dest.write_text(json.dumps(report, indent=2) + "\n", encoding="utf-8")
    return 0

   1  # turn-effort-router: dataset card (round 2)
   2  
   3  Aggregates only. Raw prompts, answers and per-row labels are in `/home/kvn/.z0int/research/sft-round2/turn-effort-router/` (private).
   4  
   5  ## Verdict
   6  
   7  Viable as a data set. The task is hard: the best cheap baseline reaches macro-F1 0.37 on a 4-class problem. The quality label is almost always "no", so it cannot be a training target (section 6).
   8  
   9  ## 1. Task
  10  
  11  Input: the first prompt of an agent turn, plus five fields known before the turn starts (harness, role, turn index, prompt length in characters, prompt kind).
  12  Output: JSON `{"effort": "<bucket>"}` with bucket = number of tool calls the agent makes before the next human prompt: `0-2`, `3-10`, `11-40`, `41+`.
  13  For a subagent run, the whole run is one turn (prompt, then tool calls until it ends). For Hermes `cron` turns, the same holds.
  14  
  15  ## 2. Files
  16  
  17  | File | Rows | Use |
  18  |---|---|---|
  19  | `data/train.jsonl` (private dir) | 5,578 | SFT train |
  20  | `data/eval.jsonl` (private dir) | 1,040 | held-out eval |
  21  
  22  Row format: `{"id", "messages": [system, user, assistant], "meta": {...}}`. The trainer reads `messages` only. `meta` holds split, source, harness, role, kind, session, cluster, ts, n_tools, bucket, prompt_chars, and the quality labels.
  23  The user message is capped at the first 1,200 and last 400 characters of the prompt, so rows stay under about 600 tokens.
  24  
  25  Code and scorer: `/mnt/zer0models/z0-wt/salvage/sft-round2/turn-effort-router/` (`run_all.sh` lists the order).
  26  
  27  ## 3. Sources and counts
  28  
  29  | Source | Raw turns found | Notes |
  30  |---|---|---|
  31  | Claude Code main thread (`~/.claude-home/projects`) | 1,809 | Kevin-typed turns plus agent turns |
  32  | Claude Code subagent runs | 1,590 | Workflow-script prompts. Mostly 11-40 and 41+ |
  33  | Codex main turns (`~/.codex/sessions`) | 2,224 | Includes goal-continuation prompts (reduced to the objective text) |
  34  | Hermes `state.db` x5 (root, chiefstaff, clean, intake, loo) | 6,595 | Human turns (cli, desktop, tui, telegram), subagents, cron |
  35  | Codex sub-sessions | 9,196 | Dropped: 5,369 are approval-review prompts, and 99% of all of them have 0-2 tools. Labels are not trustworthy |
  36  
  37  Round 1 used only the Claude main thread (1,532 turns) and Codex prompts (about 920). Hermes added most of the rows.
  38  
  39  Dropped before the split:
  40  - 1,379 turns from templated benchmark runs (11 sdk-cli sessions, each repeating the same 113 prompts).
  41  - 132 exact duplicate rows (bulk-imported messages with one timestamp).
  42  - 138 prompts that state a tool-call count or budget (for example "count your tool calls", "stop at 25 tool calls"). The label is then a function of the prompt text.
  43  - Task notifications, command echoes, hook feedback, compaction summaries and other injected messages. These do not start a turn. Their tool calls count toward the turn that is running.
  44  - Everything after 2026-10-15 00:00 UTC (turns still in progress).
  45  
  46  ## 4. Split and de-duplication
  47  
  48  - Session level split. A session id appears in one split only. A subagent run carries its parent session id.
  49  - Temporal split per harness family. Eval = the newest sessions of each family until at least 15% of that family's rows. Train rows that start after the family cut are dropped (5 rows).
  50    - Claude: eval sessions start on or after 2026-10-08. Only 11 Claude sessions qualify, one of them large, so the Claude cut cannot be finer.
  51    - Codex: on or after 2026-09-05. Hermes: on or after 2026-10-12.
  52  - Near-duplicate removal:
  53    1. Word 3-gram Jaccard >= 0.7 forms clusters (MinHash LSH, exact check). The pool (10,690 turns after the exclusions below) forms about 5,600 clusters.
  54    2. Eval keeps 1 row per cluster. Train keeps at most 4 random rows per cluster.
  55    3. 60 train rows that share a cluster with an eval row are removed.
  56    4. A second, independent check (character 5-gram Jaccard) removed 4 more eval rows (neighbour in train >= 0.7).
  57  - Result: eval is 1,040 rows (15.7% of the final 6,618), 187 sessions, 1,040 clusters, newest turn 2026-10-14. Train is 5,578 rows, 759 sessions, 4,474 clusters, 2026-07-03 to 2026-10-12.
  58  
  59  | | train | eval |
  60  |---|---|---|
  61  | 0-2 | 1,526 | 202 |
  62  | 3-10 | 1,403 | 247 |
  63  | 11-40 | 1,400 | 333 |
  64  | 41+ | 1,249 | 258 |
  65  
  66  Rows by harness and role (train / eval): Hermes main 3,681 / 244; Hermes subagent 552 / 173; Hermes cron 26 / 0; Claude main 206 / 193; Claude subagent 555 / 211; Codex main 558 / 219.
  67  The mix differs between the splits, and the label depends strongly on role. Hermes main turns are 3% 41+ in eval (8 of 244) while Hermes subagent turns are 78% 41+ (135 of 173). Per-slice scores are printed by the scorer.
  68  
  69  ## 5. Baselines on the eval set (macro-F1 over the 4 buckets, 95% cluster-bootstrap CI)
  70  
  71  Lookup tables for the first four are fitted on train only. Nothing is tuned on eval.
  72  
  73  | Baseline | macro-F1 | 95% CI | accuracy | recall 41+ |
  74  |---|---|---|---|---|
  75  | Majority class | 0.081 | 0.072-0.089 | 0.194 | 0.00 |
  76  | Metadata prior (harness, role, kind) | 0.332 | 0.308-0.355 | 0.378 | 0.71 |
  77  | Prompt-length rule (log2 bins of characters) | 0.299 | 0.275-0.322 | 0.337 | 0.65 |
  78  | Keyword rule (light-start flag plus count of "heavy" verbs) | 0.281 | 0.255-0.307 | 0.299 | 0.29 |
  79  | Naive Bayes on words (reference) | 0.369 | 0.339-0.397 | 0.373 | 0.58 |
  80  
  81  Chance for 4 classes is 0.25. The metadata prior is the best of the required baselines. It already carries most of the signal: role and harness tell you that a subagent run is long.
  82  
  83  Learnability probe (no SFT): frozen `qwen3-embedding:0.6b` on the user message plus a softmax head with metadata features, fitted on train (`embed_probe.py`; the L2 strength was chosen on the newest 20% of train, never on eval).
  84  
  85  | Probe | macro-F1 | 95% CI | accuracy | recall 41+ | vs metadata prior (paired CI) | vs naive Bayes (paired CI) |
  86  |---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
  87  | Embedding + head | 0.368 | 0.342-0.396 | 0.382 | 0.58 | +0.036 (+0.004 to +0.070) | -0.001 (-0.033 to +0.032) |
  88  
  89  Per class F1: 0-2 0.53, 3-10 0.34, 11-40 0.14, 41+ 0.46. The 11-40 bucket is the weak spot (recall 0.09). Per slice accuracy is lowest for Claude subagents (0.23). The probe passes the PASS gate by a thin margin and not the STRONG gate. So the data holds a signal beyond the harness/role prior, but it is small. An SFT model should be judged against macro-F1 0.37, not against 0.33.
  90  
  91  ## 6. Quality label (Sonnet): could one cheap model call have answered?
  92  
  93  Question to Sonnet, per turn: given the prompt, the tools used and the final answer, could a single no-tools call to a small model, seeing only the prompt text, have produced an answer of equal usefulness? Two forms:
  94  - `cheap` (strict): prompt text only.
  95  - `cheap_ctx` (lenient): same conversation history as the agent, still no tools.
  96  
  97  Sample: 300 eval turns, 75 per effort bucket (only turns with a final answer). Plus every 0-2 turn with a final answer in train (1,281) and eval (139), so 364 eval and 1,283 train rows carry the labels. All other rows have null.

  99  | Effort bucket (eval sample, n=75 each) | strict yes | lenient yes |
 100  |---|---|---|
 101  | 0-2 | 2 (3%) | 15 (20%, 95% CI 12-30%) |
 102  | 3-10 | 0 | 1 |
 103  | 11-40 | 0 | 2 |
 104  | 41+ | 0 | 0 |
 105  
 106  Over all 0-2 turns: strict yes 12.6% in train (161 of 1,281), 4.3% in eval (6 of 139); lenient yes 34% in train (441), 20% in eval (28). The rate drops from train to eval because the eval has more Claude and Hermes agent turns.
 107

 109  - Sonnet against itself (strict question, two runs): 294 of 297 agree.

 111

 113  - Effort 0-2 does not mean a cheap model could do the job. Even in the 0-2 bucket, only about 1 turn in 5 (lenient) or 1 in 25 (strict) qualifies.

1  #!/usr/bin/env python3
   2  """Scorer for turn-effort-router.
   3  
   4  Usage:
   5    score.py --eval eval.jsonl --pred preds.jsonl [--train train.jsonl] [--json out.json]
   6    score.py --eval eval.jsonl --baselines-only [--train train.jsonl]
   7  
   8  preds.jsonl: one JSON object per line: {"id": <eval row id>, "pred": "0-2"|"3-10"|"11-40"|"41+"}
   9               or {"id": ..., "text": <raw model output>}; the bucket is parsed from {"effort": "..."} or the first bucket token.
  10               A missing id or an unparseable output counts as WRONG (never dropped) and is reported as parse_fail.
  11  
  12  Primary metric: macro-F1 over the 4 effort buckets, with a 95% CI from a cluster bootstrap (resample near-duplicate
  13  clusters, 2000 draws, seed 0). Secondary: accuracy, recall of the 41+ bucket, adjacent accuracy, mean abs bucket error.
  14  Baselines are computed on the same eval rows from the train file: majority, metadata prior (harness/role/kind),
  15  prompt-length rule, keyword rule (all four are lookup tables fitted on TRAIN only; nothing is tuned on eval), and a
  16  multinomial naive-Bayes bag-of-words reference.
  17  
  18  GATE (pass condition for an SFT/router candidate):
  19    PASS   = paired cluster-bootstrap 95% CI lower bound of (model macro-F1 - best of {prior, length, keyword}) > 0
  20             AND recall(41+) >= 0.50 AND parse_fail <= 5%.
  21    STRONG = PASS AND model macro-F1 point estimate >= naive-Bayes reference.
  22  """
  23  import json, sys, re, math, argparse, collections, random, os
  24  import numpy as np
  25  
  26  B = ['0-2', '3-10', '11-40', '41+']
  27  BI = {b: i for i, b in enumerate(B)}
  28  DEF_TRAIN = os.path.expanduser('~/.z0int/research/sft-round2/turn-effort-router/data/train.jsonl')
  29  
  30  
  31  def load(p):
  32      return [json.loads(l) for l in open(p) if l.strip()]
  33  
  34  
  35  def parse_pred(d):
  36      if d is None: return None
  37      if d.get('pred') in BI: return d['pred']
  38      t = d.get('text') if d.get('text') is not None else d.get('pred')
  39      if not isinstance(t, str): return None
  40      m = re.search(r'"effort"\s*:\s*"(0-2|3-10|11-40|41\+)"', t)
  41      if m: return m.group(1)
  42      m = re.search(r'(?<![\d-])(0-2|3-10|11-40|41\+)(?![\d-])', t)
  43      return m.group(1) if m else None
  44  
  45  
  46  def user_text(r):
  47      return r['messages'][1]['content']
  48  
  49  
  50  def prompt_of(r):
  51      u = user_text(r)
  52      return u.split('\n---\n', 1)[1] if '\n---\n' in u else u
  53  
  54  
  55  def head_field(r, name, default=''):
  56      m = re.search(r'^%s: (.*)$' % name, user_text(r), re.M)
  57      return m.group(1).strip() if m else default
  58  
  59  
  60  def macro_f1(y, p):
  61      """y, p: int arrays; p == -1 means no valid prediction (counts as wrong for recall, adds no TP)."""
  62      f = []
  63      for k in range(4):
  64          tp = np.sum((y == k) & (p == k)); fp = np.sum((y != k) & (p == k)); fn = np.sum((y == k) & (p != k))
  65          f.append(0.0 if tp == 0 else 2 * tp / (2 * tp + fp + fn))
  66      return float(np.mean(f))
  67  
  68  
  69  def metrics(y, p):
  70      ok = p >= 0
  71      m41 = y == 3
  72      return {
  73          'macro_f1': macro_f1(y, p),
  74          'accuracy': float(np.mean(y == p)),
  75          'recall_41plus': float(np.mean(p[m41] == 3)) if m41.any() else float('nan'),
  76          'adjacent_acc': float(np.mean(ok & (np.abs(y - p) <= 1))),
  77          'mae_bucket': float(np.mean(np.where(ok, np.abs(y - p), 3))),
  78          'parse_fail': float(np.mean(~ok)),
  79      }
  80  
  81  
  82  def per_class(y, p):
  83      out = {}
  84      for k in range(4):
  85          tp = int(np.sum((y == k) & (p == k))); fp = int(np.sum((y != k) & (p == k))); fn = int(np.sum((y == k) & (p != k)))
  86          pr = tp / (tp + fp) if tp + fp else 0.0; rc = tp / (tp + fn) if tp + fn else 0.0
  87          out[B[k]] = {'n': int(np.sum(y == k)), 'precision': round(pr, 3), 'recall': round(rc, 3),
  88                       'f1': round(2 * pr * rc / (pr + rc), 3) if pr + rc else 0.0}
  89      return out
  90  
  91  
  92  def boot_idx(clusters, nboot=2000, seed=0):
  93      cl = collections.defaultdict(list)
  94      for i, c in enumerate(clusters): cl[c].append(i)
  95      keys = list(cl); arrs = [np.array(cl[k]) for k in keys]
  96      rng = random.Random(seed); n = len(keys)
  97      return [np.concatenate([arrs[rng.randrange(n)] for _ in range(n)]) for _ in range(nboot)]
  98  
  99  
 100  def ci(vals):
 101      v = np.asarray(vals, float); v = v[~np.isnan(v)]
 102      return float(np.percentile(v, 2.5)), float(np.percentile(v, 97.5))
 103  
 104  
 105  # ---------------- baselines (fitted on train only) ----------------
 106  LIGHT = re.compile(r'^\s*(what|why|how|is|are|does|do|did|can you explain|explain|hi|hey|ok|okay|yes|yeah|yea|yep|no|thanks|thank|sure|cool|lol|nice|wait|so)\b', re.I)
 107  HEAVY = re.compile(r'\b(implement|build|refactor|migrat\w*|audit|investigat\w*|end[- ]to[- ]end|review|verify|verif\w+|run (the )?(full )?tests?|worktree|branch|pull request|deploy|set ?up|install|research|benchmark|repo(sitory)?|codebase|every|all of|all the|fix|debug|write|create|generate|test|commit|merge|integrate|wire)\b', re.I)
 108  
 109  
 110  def kw_cell(r):
 111      p = prompt_of(r); n = len(p)
 112      hits = min(len(HEAVY.findall(p[:3000])), 6)
 113      return ('light' if LIGHT.match(p) and n < 300 else 'plain', min(hits, 6))
 114  
 115  
 116  def len_cell(r):
 117      n = len(prompt_of(r))
 118      return int(min(9, math.log2(max(n, 1))))  # log2 bins of prompt characters
 119  
 120  
 121  def meta_cell(r):
 122      return (head_field(r, 'harness'), head_field(r, 'role'), head_field(r, 'kind'))
 123  
 124  
 125  def table(train, cellf):
 126      t = collections.defaultdict(collections.Counter)
 127      for r in train: t[cellf(r)][gold(r)] += 1
 128      glob = collections.Counter()
 129      for c in t.values(): glob.update(c)
 130      gmaj = glob.most_common(1)[0][0]
 131      return {k: v.most_common(1)[0][0] for k, v in t.items()}, gmaj
 132  
 133  
 134  def apply_table(rows, cellf, tab, gmaj):
 135      return np.array([tab.get(cellf(r), gmaj) for r in rows])
 136  
 137  
 138  def gold(r):
 139      return BI[json.loads(r['messages'][2]['content'])['effort']]
 140  
 141  
 142  class NB:
 143      TOK = re.compile(r'[a-z_]{3,}')
 144  
 145      def __init__(self, train, alpha=0.5, maxf=20000):
 146          self.alpha = alpha
 147          df = collections.Counter()
 148          docs = [(gold(r), set(self.TOK.findall(prompt_of(r)[:2000].lower()))) for r in train]
 149          for _, s in docs: df.update(s)
 150          self.vocab = {w: i for i, (w, c) in enumerate(df.most_common(maxf)) if c >= 3}
 151          V = len(self.vocab); self.cnt = np.zeros((4, V)); self.prior = np.zeros(4)
 152          for y, s in docs:
 153              self.prior[y] += 1
 154              for w in s:
 155                  if w in self.vocab: self.cnt[y, self.vocab[w]] += 1
 156          self.prior = np.log((self.prior + 1) / (self.prior.sum() + 4))
 157          tot = self.prior * 0 + (self.cnt.sum(1) + alpha * V)
 158          self.logp = np.log(self.cnt + alpha) - np.log(tot)[:, None]
 159  
 160      def predict(self, rows):
 161          out = []
 162          for r in rows:
 163              idx = [self.vocab[w] for w in set(self.TOK.findall(prompt_of(r)[:2000].lower())) if w in self.vocab]
 164              out.append(int(np.argmax(self.prior + self.logp[:, idx].sum(1))))
 165          return np.array(out)
 166  
 167  
 168  def baseline_preds(train, ev):
 169      out = {}
 170      maj = collections.Counter(gold(r) for r in train).most_common(1)[0][0]
 171      out['majority'] = np.full(len(ev), maj)
 172      for name, f in (('metadata_prior', meta_cell), ('length_rule', len_cell), ('keyword_rule', kw_cell)):
 173          tab, g = table(train, f); out[name] = apply_table(ev, f, tab, g)
 174      out['naive_bayes_ref'] = NB(train).predict(ev)
 175      return out
 176  
 177  
 178  def main():
 179      ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()
 180      ap.add_argument('--eval', required=True); ap.add_argument('--pred'); ap.add_argument('--train', default=DEF_TRAIN)
 181      ap.add_argument('--json'); ap.add_argument('--baselines-only', action='store_true'); ap.add_argument('--nboot', type=int, default=2000)
 182      ap.add_argument('--cluster-by', default='session', choices=['session', 'cluster'],
 183                      help='bootstrap unit: meta.session (default, iter2) or near-duplicate meta.cluster (iter1 behaviour, was a row bootstrap)')
 184      ap.add_argument('--exclude-session', default=None, help='drop eval rows whose meta.session starts with this prefix (secondary eval)')
 185      a = ap.parse_args()
 186      ev = load(a.eval); train = load(a.train)
 187      if a.exclude_session:
 188          ev = [r for r in ev if not str(r['meta'].get('session', '')).startswith(a.exclude_session)]
 189      y = np.array([gold(r) for r in ev]); clusters = [r['meta'][a.cluster_by] for r in ev]
 190      idx = boot_idx(clusters, a.nboot)
 191      base = baseline_preds(train, ev)
 192      res = {'n_eval': len(ev), 'n_clusters': len(set(clusters)), 'eval_bucket_counts': {b: int(np.sum(y == i)) for i, b in enumerate(B)}, 'baselines': {}}
 193  
 194      def boot_stat(p):
 195          return [macro_f1(y[i], p[i]) for i in idx]
 196      bs = {}
 197      for name, p in base.items():
 198          m = metrics(y, p); bs[name] = boot_stat(p)
 199          lo, hi = ci(bs[name]); m['macro_f1_ci95'] = [round(lo, 4), round(hi, 4)]
 200          r41 = [float(np.mean(p[i][y[i] == 3] == 3)) if (y[i] == 3).any() else np.nan for i in idx]
 201          lo2, hi2 = ci(r41); m['recall_41plus_ci95'] = [round(lo2, 4), round(hi2, 4)]
 202          res['baselines'][name] = {k: (round(v, 4) if isinstance(v, float) else v) for k, v in m.items()}
 203      gate_baselines = ['metadata_prior', 'length_rule', 'keyword_rule']
 204      best = max(gate_baselines, key=lambda n: res['baselines'][n]['macro_f1'])
 205      res['best_gate_baseline'] = best
 206      print('eval rows %d, clusters %d, buckets %s' % (len(ev), res['n_clusters'], res['eval_bucket_counts']))
 207      print('%-18s %8s %-17s %8s %8s %8s' % ('baseline', 'macroF1', '95% CI', 'acc', 'rec41+', 'adj'))
 208      for n, m in res['baselines'].items():
 209          print('%-18s %8.3f [%5.3f, %5.3f] %8.3f %8.3f %8.3f' % (n, m['macro_f1'], *m['macro_f1_ci95'], m['accuracy'], m['recall_41plus'], m['adjacent_acc']))
 210      if a.baselines_only or not a.pred:
 211          if a.json: json.dump(res, open(a.json, 'w'), indent=1)
 212          return
 213      preds = {}
 214      for d in load(a.pred): preds[d['id']] = d
 215      p = np.array([BI.get(parse_pred(preds.get(r['id'])), -1) for r in ev])
 216      m = metrics(y, p); st = boot_stat(p)
 217      lo, hi = ci(st); m['macro_f1_ci95'] = [lo, hi]
 218      r41 = [float(np.mean(p[i][y[i] == 3] == 3)) if (y[i] == 3).any() else np.nan for i in idx]
 219      m['recall_41plus_ci95'] = list(ci(r41))
 220      diff = [a_ - b_ for a_, b_ in zip(st, bs[best])]
 221      dlo, dhi = ci(diff)
 222      nb_d = [a_ - b_ for a_, b_ in zip(st, bs['naive_bayes_ref'])]
 223      res['model'] = {k: (round(v, 4) if isinstance(v, float) else [round(x, 4) for x in v] if isinstance(v, list) else v) for k, v in m.items()}
 224      res['model']['per_class'] = per_class(y, p)
 225      res['model']['diff_vs_best_gate_baseline'] = {'baseline': best, 'macro_f1_diff': round(m['macro_f1'] - res['baselines'][best]['macro_f1'], 4), 'ci95': [round(dlo, 4), round(dhi, 4)]}
 226      res['model']['diff_vs_naive_bayes'] = {'macro_f1_diff': round(m['macro_f1'] - res['baselines']['naive_bayes_ref']['macro_f1'], 4), 'ci95': [round(x, 4) for x in ci(nb_d)]}
 227      # per harness/role slices
 228      sl = {}
 229      for key in sorted({(r['meta']['harness'], r['meta']['role']) for r in ev}):
 230          mk = np.array([(r['meta']['harness'], r['meta']['role']) == key for r in ev])
 231          if mk.sum() >= 20: sl['%s/%s' % key] = {'n': int(mk.sum()), 'macro_f1': round(macro_f1(y[mk], p[mk]), 3), 'accuracy': round(float(np.mean(y[mk] == p[mk])), 3)}
 232      res['model']['slices'] = sl
 233      # advisory quality: among rows predicted 0-2 that carry a Sonnet quality label
 234      q = [(r['meta'].get('cheap_ctx'), r['meta'].get('cheap')) for r, pp in zip(ev, p) if pp == 0 and r['meta'].get('cheap_ctx') in ('yes', 'no')]
 235      res['model']['advisory_cheap_among_pred_0_2'] = {'n_labelled': len(q), 'cheap_ctx_yes': sum(1 for c, _ in q if c == 'yes'), 'cheap_strict_yes': sum(1 for _, c in q if c == 'yes')}
 236      gate_pass = dlo > 0 and m['recall_41plus'] >= 0.5 and m['parse_fail'] <= 0.05
 237      res['gate'] = {'PASS': bool(gate_pass), 'STRONG': bool(gate_pass and m['macro_f1'] >= res['baselines']['naive_bayes_ref']['macro_f1']),
 238                     'conditions': {'paired_ci_lower_gt_0': dlo > 0, 'recall_41plus_ge_0.5': m['recall_41plus'] >= 0.5, 'parse_fail_le_5pct': m['parse_fail'] <= 0.05}}
 239      print('\nMODEL macro-F1 %.3f  95%% CI [%.3f, %.3f]   acc %.3f  recall41+ %.3f  adj-acc %.3f  parse_fail %.3f' %
 240            (m['macro_f1'], lo, hi, m['accuracy'], m['recall_41plus'], m['adjacent_acc'], m['parse_fail']))
 241      print('vs best gate baseline (%s): diff %+.3f  paired 95%% CI [%+.3f, %+.3f]' % (best, m['macro_f1'] - res['baselines'][best]['macro_f1'], dlo, dhi))
 242      print('vs naive-bayes ref:        diff %+.3f  paired 95%% CI [%+.3f, %+.3f]' % (res['model']['diff_vs_naive_bayes']['macro_f1_diff'], *res['model']['diff_vs_naive_bayes']['ci95']))
 243      print('per class:', json.dumps(res['model']['per_class']))
 244      print('GATE:', json.dumps(res['gate']))
 245      if a.json: json.dump(res, open(a.json, 'w'), indent=1)

{"https://empryo.com/docs/concepts/genome.md":"# The Genome

> The Genome is Empryo's live, ranked map of your repository. It goes into every prompt so the agent knows where code lives before it starts searching.

The **Genome** is a map of your codebase that Empryo builds when you open a project. It lists your files, the symbols they export and how files depend on each other, ranked by importance. A compact version of the map goes at the top of every prompt.

Because the agent can see the map, it rarely needs to spend a turn asking "where does auth live?" It starts from the right files.

## What the agent sees

A slice of the map looks like this:

```
src/services/auth/session.ts (→12)
 +SessionManager Tracks active sessions, refresh tokens, expiry
 +SessionStore
```

- `+` marks an exported symbol.
- `(→12)` means 12 other files depend on this one.
- `[NEW]` marks a file changed in the last 48 hours.
- The text after a symbol name is a one-line summary, when summaries are on.

## How files are ranked

- **Dependencies.** Files that many other files import rank higher.
- **Your current work.** Files you just edited or mentioned get a boost for that turn.
- **Git history.** Files that usually change together are pulled in together.
- **Live updates.** When a file changes, the map is updated right away.

The scanner understands dozens of languages and file formats, including TypeScript, JavaScript, Python, Rust, Go, Java, C, C++, C#, Ruby, PHP, Swift and Kotlin.

## Settings

The Genome works without any setup. Open `/genome` to see its status, rebuild or clear the index, or turn it off.

To change it in config:

```json
{
 "genome": true,
 "semanticSummaries": "synthetic"
}
```

| Key | Values |
|-----|--------|
| `genome` | `true` (default), or `false` to turn the map off |
| `semanticSummaries` | `"synthetic"` (free, derived from code and names), `"ast"` (docstrings only), `"llm"` (short model-written descriptions, costs tokens), `"full"`, or `"off"` |

## What gets scanned

The scan sees what git sees: tracked and untracked files, minus anything your `.gitignore` excludes. Build output (`node_modules`, `dist`, `build`, `target`, `coverage` and similar) and dot-directories such as `.github` are skipped even if they are tracked. Outside a git repository, the same rules apply to a plain folder scan.

To bring a dot-directory back, negate it in `.empryoignore`, for example `!Configs/.local/`. Build output and internal folders such as `.git` stay out either way.

### Keep files out of the map

Some files should stay in git but not in the map: test fixtures, benchmark inputs, a folder of SVGs. List them in a **`.empryoignore`** file at the project root. It uses the same syntax as `.gitignore`, including `!` negations and `**`:

```gitignore
# Keep these in git, but out of the Genome
testenvs/
bench/
assets/
public/
```

Some files stay out in every project without any `.empryoignore`: package lockfiles (`bun.lock`, `package-lock.json`, `Cargo.lock` and the like), minified and bundled JavaScript, test snapshots, generated protobuf and Dart files, Xcode asset catalogs, and vendored folders such as `vendor/`, `venv/`, `Pods/` and `DerivedData/`. A `!` line in `.empryoignore` brings any of them back.

What happens:

- Matching files drop out of the map and out of code-wide file listings.
- The agent can still `read` or `grep` them by explicit path. They are hidden from discovery, not blocked.
- Saving `.empryoignore` or `.gitignore` triggers a quick rescan. Unchanged files are skipped, so it takes seconds.
- If a change would remove more than 80% of the index at once, Empryo treats it as a mistake and refuses. Use **clear** in `/genome` to force a rebuild.

### Large repositories

The map holds up to 10,000 files. In bigger repositories, the most recently changed files win, and `/genome` tells you the cap was reached. Excluding noise with `.empryoignore` makes sure the cap cuts fixtures rather than source code.

## Skip the scan

For a quick one-off question in headless mode, you can skip the scan:

```bash
empryo --headless --no-genome "what's the version?"
```

Setting the environment variable `EMPRYO_NO_GENOME=1` does the same.","https://empryo.com/docs/tools/memory.md":"# Memory

> Empryo remembers your preferences, project decisions and past gotchas across sessions, and adds up to 3 relevant ones to each turn automatically.

[Video: Recall at work: Empryo scores stored memories against the current request and the files in play, then adds the three most relevant, each labeled with why it was picked.](https://empryo.com/media/code-memory-recall.mp4)

*Recall at work: Empryo scores stored memories against the current request and the files in play, then adds the three most relevant, each labeled with why it was picked.*

Memory lets Empryo remember things between sessions: that you use bun, not npm; why the team switched state libraries; that a test is flaky on CI. You tell it once, and it comes back when it matters.

Memory is stored **per project** by default. You can also keep **global** memories that apply to every project, such as "be terse".

## What gets stored

Each memory has one of four categories:

| Category | Example |
|---|---|
| `pref` | "use bun not npm", "be terse" |
| `decision` | "switched to zustand because redux was too much boilerplate" |
| `gotcha` | "JWT expiry uses the container clock, which drifts in prod" |
| `context` | "legacy/ will be deleted next sprint, don't touch it" |

The agent saves a memory on its own when you state a preference, make a decision with a reason, or hit a bug that wasn't obvious. You can also ask it directly: "remember that we deploy on Thursdays".

[Video: Left: a rules file sent in full on every turn, outdated lines included. Right: Empryo adds three short memories that match the file being edited.](https://empryo.com/media/code-memory-prompt-bloat.mp4)

*Left: a rules file sent in full on every turn, outdated lines included. Right: Empryo adds three short memories that match the file being edited.*

## How recall works

Before each turn, Empryo compares your message and the files you are working on with what's stored. It adds up to **3 relevant memories** to the turn. You don't need to run a command or remember what's saved.

If nothing is relevant, nothing is added. Memories only take up space in the conversation when they help.

## Browse and edit: `/memory`

In the terminal UI, run `/memory` to open the memory browser. It has four tabs:

- **All:** every memory you can see, from the project and global stores. Pin, edit or hide a memory from here.
- **Hidden:** memories you hid. Restore them with `Ctrl+R`.
- **Cleanup:** suggestions to review, such as duplicates, memories that point at deleted files, and memories that are rarely useful.
- **Settings:** which stores the agent reads from and writes to, and which embedding model is in use.

Hiding a memory is reversible. **Purge all** (`Ctrl+X`) deletes permanently, so use it with care.

The desktop app has a Memory pane with the same data.

## Scopes

Memories live in two databases:

| Scope | Location | Use it for |
|---|---|---|
| Project | `.empryo/memory.db` in the repository | Decisions and gotchas about this code |
| Global | `~/.empryo/memory.db` | Your personal preferences and style |

New memories go to the project store by default. The read scope controls what recall can see:

```
all project + global (default)
project only this repository
global only your global preferences
none recall off
```

Change both in `/memory` → **Settings**.

## Pinning

Pin a memory to keep it out of cleanup suggestions and rank it higher in recall. Pin the rules you never want the agent to miss.

## Languages

Memory search works in any language or script, including Chinese, Japanese, Arabic and Cyrillic, and mixed-script identifiers. It matches both whole words and parts of words, so rephrased and non-English queries still find the right memory.

## Better matching with an embedding model

By default, Empryo uses a built-in offline embedder. It needs no API key and makes no network calls. It matches memories well when your wording overlaps with what was stored.

For better matching of rephrased text, point memory at an embedding model:

```json
{
 "memory": {
 "embeddingModel": "openai/text-embedding-3-small"
 }
}
```

### Do I need an API key?

Yes, for a hosted model. Empryo uses the key you already configured for that provider. For `openai/text-embedding-3-small`, that is your OpenAI key. If the key is missing or wrong, Empryo falls back to the offline embedder and memory keeps working. `/memory` → **Settings** shows the reason.

Local models in Ollama or LM Studio need no key. Pull the model, then name it in the config.

### Which models can I use?

Any `provider/model` ID whose provider offers embeddings:

| Provider | Model |
|---|---|
| OpenAI | `openai/text-embedding-3-small`, `openai/text-embedding-3-large` |
| Google | `google/text-embedding-004` |
| Mistral | `mistral/mistral-embed` |
| OpenRouter | `openrouter/openai/text-embedding-3-small` |
| Vercel AI Gateway | `vercel_gateway/openai/text-embedding-3-small` |
| Ollama (local) | `ollama/nomic-embed-text`, `ollama/mxbai-embed-large` |
| LM Studio (local) | `lmstudio/nomic-embed-text` |

Providers without an embeddings API, such as Anthropic, xAI, Groq, DeepSeek and Bedrock, use the offline embedder instead. Custom OpenAI-compatible providers work if they expose an `/embeddings` endpoint.

If you don't set `embeddingModel`, Empryo picks one in this order: your `taskRouter.semantic` model, then a default for your current chat provider (OpenAI, Google, OpenRouter or Vercel AI Gateway), then the offline embedder. Set `"embeddingModel": null` to always use the offline embedder.

### How do I check it's working?

Open `/memory` → **Settings** and look at the **Embedding** row. It shows the model in use and where the choice came from. # MCP Servers

> Connect Empryo to Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers over stdio, HTTP or SSE, so the agent can use their tools next to the built-in ones.

MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open standard for giving AI agents extra tools. Connect an MCP server to Empryo and the agent can call its tools, for example to open GitHub issues or query Sentry, alongside its built-in tools.

Use it when the agent needs a service Empryo does not cover out of the box.

## Quick start

Add a server to `mcpServers` in your config. This one runs the GitHub server as a local process:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": [
    {
      "name": "github",
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-github"],
      "env": { "GITHUB_TOKEN": "ghp_..." }
    }
  ]
}
```

Restart Empryo or open `/mcp` to check it connected. The server's tools are now available to the agent as `mcp__github__<tool>`.

If you copy a config from another tool that writes `mcpServers` as an object keyed by server name, that works too. Empryo reads the key as the server's `name`.

## Where the config lives

- **Global:** `~/.empryo/config.json` applies to every project.
- **Project:** `.empryo/config.json` applies to one repository. A project server with the same `name` as a global one replaces it.

A project's MCP servers start only after you trust the repository with `/trust`. This stops a cloned repo from running commands on your machine without your say.

## Three ways to connect

| Transport | Use it for | Needs |
|---|---|---|
| `stdio` (default) | A server that runs as a local program | `command`, optional `args`, `env`, `cwd` |
| `http` | A remote server over Streamable HTTP. Use this for new remote servers | `url`, optional `headers` |
| `sse` | Older remote servers that only speak Server-Sent Events | `url`, optional `headers` |

```json
{
  "mcpServers": [
    {
      "name": "sentry",
      "transport": "http",
      "url": "https://mcp.sentry.dev/sse",
      "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer ..." }
    },
    {
      "name": "legacy-service",
      "transport": "sse",
      "url": "https://legacy.example.com/events",
      "disabled": true
    }
  ]
}
```

## Settings

| Field | Type | What it does |
|-------|------|-------------|
| `name` | string (required) | The server's name. Also the prefix of its tool names |
| `transport` | `"stdio"` \| `"http"` \| `"sse"` | How to connect. Default `"stdio"` |
| `command` | string | Program to start (stdio) |
| `args` | string[] | Arguments for `command` |
| `env` | `Record<string,string>` | Environment variables for the program |
| `cwd` | string | Working directory for the program (stdio) |
| `url` | string | Server address (http, sse) |
| `headers` | `Record<string,string>` | HTTP headers, such as `Authorization` (http, sse) |
| `timeout` | number | Time limit for each tool call, in ms. Default 30000 |
| `disabled` | boolean | Keep the entry but don't connect |
| `resident` | boolean | Always send this server's tools to the model instead of loading them on demand. Use it for a server you rely on every turn. The set is fixed when a session starts, so the prompt cache holds: a server pinned later, or one that was not connected at startup, is reached on demand until the next session, and a pinned server that disconnects keeps its tools, which answer that it is not connected |
| `redirect` | `"follow"` \| `"error"` | Whether a remote server may redirect. Set `"follow"` only if the server needs it |

## Tool names

Every MCP tool is renamed to `mcp__<server>__<tool>` so it can never clash with a built-in tool. A server named `github` with a tool `create_issue` gives the agent `mcp__github__create_issue`.

## Connection behavior

- All enabled servers connect when Empryo starts, up to four at a time.
- If a local (stdio) server crashes, Empryo restarts it, up to three times with a growing delay.
- A remote server that fails stays failed until you retry it from `/mcp`.
- When Empryo exits, it closes every connection and stops every local server.

## Manage servers in the terminal UI

Run `/mcp` to see each server's status and tools.

| Key | Action |
|----------|--------|
| Type | Filter servers by name |
| `Ctrl+A` | Add a server |
| `Ctrl+E` | Edit the selected server |
| `Ctrl+D` | Delete the selected server |
| `Ctrl+T` | Turn the selected server on or off |
| `Ctrl+R` | Reconnect a failed server |
| `Ctrl+P` | Ping a connected server |
| `Tab` | Switch to the tools list |
| `Enter` | Open the server's details |

## Headless runs

MCP servers also connect in headless mode, so scripts and CI jobs can use them:

```bash
empryo --headless "use the github MCP to list open issues"
```
